About the simulation

This simulation visualizes a single-qubit spin state on the Bloch sphere and shows how projective measurements along the X, Y, and Z axes collapse the state.

Use the Measure Spin buttons to perform axis measurements, Set Custom State to enter amplitudes or presets, and Reset in the header to return to the default state. The wavefunction panel and probability bars update after each action.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The Bloch sphere

Let’s get to know the picture. A spin-½ particle is drawn as the white arrow on the sphere: its tilt θ from the Z axis and its azimuth φ around that axis fix the state |ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)|↑⟩ + eiφsin(θ/2)|↓⟩. The poles are |↑⟩ and |↓⟩, and the X and Y axes carry their own pairs of states. Measuring along an axis asks the particle which of that axis’s two states it’s in.

2 · The classical picture

Let’s begin the old-fashioned way. Before quantum mechanics, a spin is just a small arrow of fixed length ℏ/2 that can point in any direction. Tilt it 60° away from the Z axis and measure its component along Z. What do you think comes back?

3 · One measurement

Now for a real quantum measurement. The arrow lies on the equator along +X, an equal mix of |↑⟩ and |↓⟩. Measure Z just once. What do you think the history will record?

4 · How often up?

Let’s put some numbers on it. The state is now |ψ⟩ = (√3/2)|↑⟩ + (1/2)|↓⟩, the arrow tilted 60° from Z. If you prepare it afresh many times and measure along Z each time, what fraction of the runs do you think give Spin Up?

5 · Measuring twice

Now for a follow-up. The arrow is back on the equator, an even mix, and a Z measurement snaps it to one pole. What do you expect a second Z measurement on that same particle to return?

6 · An X measurement in between

One last twist. The particle sits at the |↑⟩ pole, the definite Z result of a first measurement. Now measure X, then measure Z again. How do you think this second Z result compares with the first?

The Physics

Spin measurement on the Bloch sphere · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim draws the state of one spin-½ particle as an arrow on the Bloch sphere and lets you measure it along the Z, X or Y axis. With only two basis states the whole state fits in two angles, so spin is the cleanest place to study a quantum measurement.

What you'll learn

  • How a spin state is written as two angles, θ and φ, or two amplitudes, α and β.
  • What a measurement along an axis returns, and what it does to the state.
  • How the probability bars and the sphere's colours follow from the state.
  • How measurements along different axes relate to one another.
The sim's picture: a white arrow on a sphere, tilted by θ from the Z axis and turned by φ around it.

What's on screen

  • White arrow: the spin state, tilted by θ from Z and turned by φ around it.
  • Blue Z axis with the poles |↑⟩ and |↓⟩. Green X axis, |±x⟩. Amber Y axis, |±y⟩.
  • Sphere colour and its P(n̂) legend, 0% to 100% (section 06).
  • Right panel: |ψ⟩ with the P(↑) and P(↓) bars, the Bloch Coordinates, and the History.
See itTilt the spin to 60° from Z. Watch for: the white arrow leaning away from the blue Z axis, and the Bloch Coordinates line reading θ = 60.0°.

03

A state is two angles on a sphere

The two basis states |↑⟩ and |↓⟩ are the ends of the Z axis. Any state is a superposition of them, with complex amplitudes α and β:

One spin-½ state, written the way the sim's amplitude boxes hold it.
  • |α|² + |β|² = 1 fixes the size, and an overall phase changes nothing observable. Two numbers remain: θ, the tilt from +Z (0° to 180°), and φ, the phase of β relative to α.
  • The arrow points along ŝ = (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ).
  • The X axis ends are |±x⟩ = (|↑⟩ ± |↓⟩)/√2, at θ = 90° and φ = 0° or 180°. The Y axis ends are |±y⟩ = (|↑⟩ ± i|↓⟩)/√2, at θ = 90° and φ = +90° or −90°.
  • Opposite points on the sphere are orthogonal states. Only the ratio β/α matters: typing α = 1, β = 1 or α = 5, β = 5 gives the same state.
See itSet the state to |+y⟩. Watch for: the arrow lying flat on the equator along the amber Y axis, with θ = 90.0° and φ = 90.0°.
04

A measurement returns one of two values

Measuring along Z uses the operator Ŝz. It has two eigenvalues and no others:

The measured quantity has two eigenvalues; the classical projection is not one of them.
  • A classical spin of length ħ/2 tilted by θ would have a Z component (ħ/2) cos θ, anywhere from −ħ/2 to +ħ/2. At θ = 60° that is ħ/4.
  • The sim returns only +ħ/2 (↑ Spin Up in the History) or −ħ/2 (↓ Spin Down). ħ/4 never appears.
  • X and Y measurements work the same way along their own axes: two results, Spin + or Spin −, which are +ħ/2 and −ħ/2 along that axis.
  • The tilt is not lost. It sets how often each result turns up (section 06).
Left: the classical arrow, whose Z component varies continuously with the tilt. Right: the sim's Bloch sphere at θ = 60°, φ = 0.
See itTilt to 60°, then measure Z. Watch for: one new History line, either ↑ Spin Up or ↓ Spin Down, never anything in between.
05

The state lands on the result

After a measurement the sim sets the state to the eigenstate that was found. This is the projection rule of the textbook postulates:

The projection rule for a Z measurement. The sim then writes back the new θ and φ.
  • After Z: θ = 0° (↑) or 180° (↓), with φ = 0°.
  • After X: θ = 90° with φ = 0° (+x) or 180° (−x). After Y: θ = 90° with φ = +90° (+y) or −90° (−y). The arrow lands on the axis you measured.
  • Measure the same axis again and the state is already an eigenstate, so the same result comes back every time.
  • The swing takes about 0.67 s in the sim. That is animation. The sim stores one state and shows the rule, and it does not decide what physically happens in the measurement.
See itStart from |+x⟩ and measure Z twice in a row. Watch for: the two Z lines in the History carrying the same label.
06

Probability is the squared amplitude

The Born rule, in the three forms this sim evaluates.
  • For a Z measurement, P(↑) = |α|² = cos²(θ/2) and P(↓) = |β|² = sin²(θ/2). At θ = 60°, α = √3/2 ≈ 0.87 but P(↑) = 75%: the probability is the amplitude squared.
  • The bars show only the Z numbers and ignore φ: |+x⟩ and |+y⟩ both read 50 / 50.
  • For any direction n̂ the chance of "+" is P(n̂) = ½(1 + n̂·ŝ). That is the sphere's colour: the state is the white arrow, and the colour maps the answer for every axis.
  • A probability shows up as a frequency over many identical preparations. The average ⟨Ŝz⟩ = (ħ/2)[P(↑) − P(↓)] = (ħ/2) cos θ is ħ/4 at 60°, a value no single run returns.
θ φ

Drag θ and φ and the sim's α and β boxes follow. A new state is ignored while the arrow is moving, so a fast drag settles a moment later.

The two Z probabilities against θ, with ⟨Ŝz⟩/(ħ/2) dashed. Dots mark θ = 0°, 60° and 90°.
See itPrepare the 60° state afresh and measure Z eight times. Watch for: mostly ↑ Spin Up lines, about 6 of 8 expected, yet every single run still gives one of the two results.
07

Different axes cannot both be sharp

Z, X and Y measurements each have two results, but they do not share eigenstates. The operators do not commute, and an uncertainty relation follows:

Non-commuting observables, and the uncertainty relation that follows.
  • |↑⟩ has a certain Z result. An X measurement on it returns + or − with probability ½ each, and the state lands on the equator, where P(↑) = ½. The earlier certainty about Z is gone.
  • The sim implements one rule: a stored state, and results drawn at random with the Born probabilities. It has no hidden value behind a result.
  • Whether a pre-existing value could still exist is decided by Bell-type experiments on entangled pairs. This one-spin sim cannot address that.
See itStart at |↑⟩ and measure X. Watch for: P(↑) falling from 100% to 50% once the X result arrives.
08

Where it matters

The Stern–Gerlach experiment: spin-½ atoms arrive as two spots, not a band.
  • Stern–Gerlach, 1922. Silver atoms crossed a magnetic field that varies along Z. A classical spread of tilts predicts a smear; the plate showed two spots. A Z measurement in this sim is that experiment.
  • NMR and MRI. Proton spin states split in a magnetic field, and the transition frequency is f = (γ/2π)B with γ/2π = 42.58 MHz/T, about 128 MHz at 3 T. This sim has no field or time evolution.
  • Qubits. |ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + eiφ sin(θ/2)|1⟩ is the state of section 03 with new labels, and reading out a qubit is a Z measurement.
Go deeper: any measurement axis
  • Measuring along a unit vector n̂ uses Ŝn = n̂·Ŝ. Its results are ±ħ/2, with probabilities P(±) = ½(1 ± n̂·ŝ).
  • The sim's three buttons are n̂ = ẑ, x̂ and ŷ. The sphere colour is P(+) for every n̂ on the sphere.
09

Summary

In one line. A spin state is a direction on the sphere. A measurement along n̂ returns +ħ/2 or −ħ/2 with probabilities ½(1 ± n̂·ŝ), and leaves the state on the result.

Key points

  • A state is θ and φ, or α and β with |α|² + |β|² = 1.
  • A Z measurement returns +ħ/2 or −ħ/2, with P(↑) = cos²(θ/2).
  • The same axis again repeats the result; another axis re-randomises it.

Common mix-ups

  • "Tilt it 60° and a Z measurement reads ħ/4." Every reading is +ħ/2 or −ħ/2. ħ/4 is only the average.
  • "The amplitude is the probability." √3/2 ≈ 0.87 is the amplitude. The probability is its square, 0.75.
  • "The coloured sphere shows where the spin is." The state is the white arrow. The colour is P(n̂) for each axis.

Things to try on your own

  • Apply α = 1, β = 1, then α = 1, β = i. Compare the Z bars, then measure X on each.
  • Use the sliders in section 06 to find the θ at which P(↑) = 25%, then confirm it with Z measurements.
  • From |↑⟩ press X, then Z. Repeat a few times and count the ↑ results.
